hero.name: Anna Burgess
hero.headline: Mechanical design, manufacturing, robotics, propulsion, controls, and hands-on engineering.
hero.intro: I’m a Mechanical Engineering student at Harvard focused on taking systems from analysis and CAD through machining, assembly, testing, and iteration. My work spans liquid rocketry, robotics, computational mechanics, controls, research hardware, manufacturing, and personal fabrication.

about.title: Engineering from first principles to hardware.
paragraphs: I am pursuing a B.S. in Mechanical Engineering at Harvard College with a minor in Mathematical Sciences. My coursework includes computer-aided machine design, mechanical systems, solid and computational mechanics, and robotics.

My experience is strongly fabrication-driven: manual and CNC machining, welding, 3D printing, laser and waterjet cutting, soldering, CAD/CAE, embedded controls, fixture design, testing, and iterative build work.
Outside coursework, I lead and contribute to rocketry and robotics programs, work in research environments, and build personal projects ranging from CNC equipment to vehicle restoration.

fud.title: Forward Unto Dawn — Regeneratively Cooled Liquid Bipropellant Engine
fud.summary: Liquid bipropellant engine development centered on regenerative cooling, an additively manufactured combustion chamber, and analytical validation.
fud.desc: Forward Unto Dawn is a student-designed regeneratively cooled liquid bipropellant engine. The project was initially proposed in Spring 2026, then suspended as the team prioritized IREC. It later continued as an independent summer effort led by another club member.
fud.contrib: Managed project progress and served as the primary design reviewer during the summer continuation, reviewing propulsion math, simulations, CAD, and other engineering work as the design developed.

deepDive.label: Analytical Development
deepDive.content: Review of the propulsion math and simulations used to support the regeneratively cooled engine design.

deepDive.label: CAD Development
deepDive.content: Review of CAD development and mechanical implementation as the engine architecture progressed.

deepDive.label: Manufacturing
deepDive.content: Manufacturing planning and hardware development for the student-designed engine, including consideration of the additively manufactured combustion-chamber approach.

deepDive.label: Design Reviews
deepDive.content: Acted as the primary reviewer for ongoing design work, reviewing calculations, simulations, CAD, and overall project progress.

rocketlink.title: RocketLink Telemetry System
rocketlink.summary: Long-range LoRa/GPS telemetry system developed through breadboard, protoboard, and PCB-based iterations with custom avionics housings.
rocketlink.desc: RocketLink is a long-range telemetry project developed to transmit rocket position and flight data using LoRa and GPS hardware. The system evolved through multiple hardware and enclosure iterations as the team tested mechanical robustness, packaging, and field usability.
rocketlink.contrib: Worked from the initial payload requirements through enclosure design and iterative hardware integration. Designed the printed housings, packaged the transmitter and receiver electronics, incorporated feedback from field testing, and revised the mechanical design between V1 and V2.

deepDive.label: Concept Design
deepDive.content: Met with an alumni mentor to define what the telemetry payload needed to accomplish and translated those requirements into an initial electronics and packaging concept.

deepDive.label: Prototyping & Testing
deepDive.content: The first system was assembled on a breadboard and tested outdoors at Harvard SEC. Later validation requirements included making the system robust enough to tolerate aggressive field testing, including operation while held outside a moving vehicle.

deepDive.label: V1
deepDive.content: V1 used independently wired and soldered components on a protoboard. The protoboard was secured in a PLA housing with press-fit hex nuts. A separate battery compartment used Velcro routed through 3D-printed rings, while dedicated openings provided access for the antenna, GPS module, and battery wiring. A corresponding receiver enclosure provided a cable connection for data transmission.

deepDive.label: V1 Feedback
deepDive.content: Testing showed that the wired connections and overall assembly were too mechanically fragile for the intended field environment, motivating a more robust electrical architecture and enclosure revision.

deepDive.label: V2
deepDive.content: V2 replaced the individually wired protoboard architecture with a custom PCB to eliminate weak soldered wire connections. The battery was moved outside the enclosure for easier use, the GPS hardware was secured more robustly, external clearances were increased, and the lid and enclosure lip were thickened to improve the slide-on cover.

sphinx.title: Mojave Sphinx Rocket + Static Test Stand
sphinx.summary: Rocket assembly, component manufacturing, and development of a dedicated engine static-test stand.
sphinx.desc: Mojave Sphinx is a documented Half Cat Rocketry liquid rocket that the team adopted as a capability-building project after encountering roadblocks with an earlier research-heavy liquid bipropellant design. The goal was to gain practical experience in machining, fluids hardware, integration, and static-fire operations before returning to more open-ended propulsion development.
sphinx.contrib: Worked extensively on subsystem and full-vehicle assembly, including servo-actuated LOX and fuel ball valves, propellant bulkheads and interface rings, the engine, avionics sled, propellant-piston installation, and full-scale integration. Drilled the large tank body and manufactured a quick disconnect. I also developed the test-stand concept and personally manufactured, assembled, and installed the stand, although I did not create its CAD model.

deepDive.label: Subsystem Assembly
deepDive.content: Assembled the servo-actuated ball valves for LOX and fuel, worked on the fuel and LOX bulkheads and their interface-ring connections, assembled the engine, and assembled the avionics sled.

deepDive.label: Full-System Assembly
deepDive.content: Oversaw propellant-piston installation and the full integration and assembly of the rocket, bringing the individual fluids, propulsion, avionics, and structural subsystems together.

deepDive.label: Test Stand Concept
deepDive.content: Developed the concept for a high-factor-of-safety static-fire stand. The installation used a buried bucket of concrete as the primary ground anchor and was planned around securely restraining the vehicle during firing.

deepDive.label: Test Stand CAD
deepDive.content: The final CAD model for the Sphinx test stand was produced by another team member. My role was concept development and then manufacturing, assembly, installation, and integration of the stand.

deepDive.label: Test Stand Manufacturing
deepDive.content: Manufactured the test stand hardware and prepared the structure for field installation.

deepDive.label: Test Stand Assembly
deepDive.content: Assembled the test stand in preparation for installation at the team test site.

deepDive.label: Test Stand Integration
deepDive.content: Installed the stand in two stages at the test site and integrated the rocket onto the stand for static-fire operations.

deepDive.label: Static Fire
deepDive.content: The rocket was secured to the stand for static-fire testing. A previous attempt was unsuccessful because of poor sealing in the fluids system; the team planned another static fire for Fall 2026.

irec.title: IREC 10K COTS Competition Rocket
irec.summary: Active development of a 10,000-ft COTS competition rocket for IREC.
irec.desc: An active effort to develop a 10,000-ft COTS competition rocket for IREC 2027. The project is currently in the planning and early design stage, with emphasis on requirements, schedule, rule compliance, and building a technically realistic path to competition.
irec.contrib: Developed the full project Gantt chart and design specifications, reviewed competition rules and relevant literature, and studied other teams’ rockets to inform planning. The next stage is CAD and OpenRocket development followed by material ordering.
irec.result: In progress — competition planned for June 2027

deepDive.label: Current Development
deepDive.content: Developed the project Gantt chart and design specifications and reviewed the relevant competition rules, literature, and prior team designs. The next planned work is CAD and OpenRocket development, followed by material ordering. Competition is planned for June 2027.

l1.title: NAR Level 1 High-Power Rocketry Certification
l1.summary: Built and launched an Apogee Zephyr to successfully earn NAR Level 1 certification.
l1.desc: A high-power rocketry certification project centered on an Apogee Zephyr. In addition to building and flying my own rocket, I reverse engineered the Zephyr geometry so the team could create a lower-cost fleet for additional Level 1 certification flights.
l1.contrib: Assembled the Zephyr, reverse engineered its geometry into SolidWorks CAD, supported fabrication of team rockets, validated vehicles in OpenRocket, and completed the full launch sequence. I earned my NAR Level 1 certification on the first launch.

deepDive.label: Assembly
deepDive.content: Assembled an Apogee Zephyr high-power rocket and prepared it for certification flight.

deepDive.label: CAD / Reverse Engineering
deepDive.content: Developed reverse-engineered SolidWorks CAD for the Zephyr to support a lower-cost team certification fleet. Where direct dimensions were unavailable, I used photographs and image ratios to estimate geometric dimensions.

deepDive.label: Manufacturing
deepDive.content: The team used laser cutting for centering rings and fins on the reverse-engineered fleet. Individual rockets were weighed and their configurations were checked before flight.

deepDive.label: Launch Procedure
deepDive.content: Validated the rocket in OpenRocket, completed the certification launch sequence, recovered the vehicle successfully, and earned NAR Level 1 High Power Rocketry certification on the first launch.

phase1.title: Phase 1 Liquid Bipropellant Rocket Design
phase1.summary: Early-stage liquid bipropellant vehicle design including bulkhead FEA, concept sketches, and structural geometry optimization.
phase1.desc: An early-phase liquid bipropellant rocket concept that explored vehicle structure, bulkhead load paths, and packaging before the program was indefinitely suspended.
phase1.contrib: Performed SolidWorks FEA on bulkheads, developed concept sketches, and used material cutaways and geometry iteration to optimize bulkhead designs.

deepDive.content: Add the prototype concepts, early experiments, and iteration path for this project.

urc.title: University Rover Challenge — Rover Manufacturing
urc.summary: Precision manufacturing for a Mars rover, including suspension and arm power-transmission hardware.
urc.desc: Manufacturing, DFM, integration, and troubleshooting work for a University Rover Challenge Mars rover. The rover required custom mechanical hardware across its suspension, arm, chassis, and other subsystems.
urc.contrib: Machined more than 30 parts, including many power-transmission components, using manual and CNC processes across four lathes and two mills. Reviewed rover parts for manufacturability, redesigned difficult features, supported integration and testing, and implemented mechanical fixes identified during system troubleshooting.

deepDive.label: Manufacturing
deepDive.content: Machined more than 30 rover components, with substantial work on power-transmission hardware, using both manual and CNC machining across four lathes and two mills.

deepDive.label: Design for Manufacturability
deepDive.content: Reviewed rover parts and proposed changes where geometry was difficult or impossible to machine with available equipment. One coupler originally required a broached feature on one side and an internal hex on the other; I added dog-ear reliefs at the hex corners so the corners could be drilled and the remaining profile machined with a SolidWorks-generated CNC program.

deepDive.label: Assembly & Integration
deepDive.content: Worked on assembly and integration of the machined hardware into the rover and supported subsystem and full-system testing.

deepDive.label: Testing & Troubleshooting
deepDive.content: Evaluated mechanical problems during testing and proposed fixes. When the differential bar had excessive play, I added an additional bearing constraint to increase rigidity. When a set-screw connection between the rocker-bogie drive system and differential suspension repeatedly loosened, I implemented Loctite to mitigate the issue.

ability.title: Servo-Driven Visual Perturbation Headset
ability.summary: Low-cost experimental headset using servo-driven mirrors to induce controlled balance perturbations.
ability.desc: Redesign of a visual-perturbation headset used in balance research. The original acrylic-and-tape assembly was replaced with a lighter, mechanically constrained, serviceable 3D-printed system.
ability.contrib: Redesigned the headset architecture in CAD, replaced taped acrylic construction with 3D-printed PLA and rigid mechanical joints, redesigned the servo-driven rotational axis and mirror retention, added PCB mounting, and iterated the assembly from captive-nut joints to heat-set inserts.

deepDive.label: Original Design
deepDive.content: The original headset was made from laser-cut acrylic and relied heavily on duct tape for assembly and retention.

deepDive.label: Structural Redesign
deepDive.content: Redesigned the headset in 3D-printed PLA using interlocking edges and captive-nut joints, then iterated again to use heat-set inserts. The rigid mechanical joints significantly improved stability, while 15% infill PLA made the assembly noticeably lighter than the 1/8-in acrylic predecessor.

deepDive.label: Servo & Rotational Axis
deepDive.content: Connected the servo to the rotational axis using captive press-fit hex hardware and screws passing through the rotational axis into the servo-side connector.

deepDive.label: Mirror Retention
deepDive.content: Both mirrors were mechanically retained through friction-based interfaces. The rotating mirror fit into a slot and was constrained by four set screws; the second mirror was clamped between two flat planes tightened together during assembly.

deepDive.label: Electronics & Weight Integration
deepDive.content: Added dedicated PCB screw mounting on top of the headset and replaced taped weight covers with black fabric retained by Velcro.

deepDive.label: CAD Architecture
deepDive.content: Built the CAD using coordinated multibody geometry: a master part defined the related bodies, while individual part and assembly models were driven from that shared geometry to preserve relationships between components.

mahi.title: Force-Sensing Wearable Hardware
mahi.summary: Equation-driven CAD and 3D-printed housings for force-sensitive resistors used in wearable sensing applications.
mahi.desc: Research on 3D-printed TPU housings and force-sensitive-resistor integration for two wearable biomedical sensing applications: a center-of-pressure sensing foot insole and a force-quantifying scoliosis brace. The work combined equation-driven CAD, multi-material additive manufacturing, electronics integration, and Instron validation.
mahi.contrib: Redesigned the insole and brace sensor architectures, developed equation-driven SolidWorks models, explored conductive TPU and embedded wiring, designed serviceable alternatives, and conducted extensive Instron validation. For the FSR experiment, I completed 125 trials and parsed the resulting data in Excel.

deepDive.label: Initial / Given Designs
deepDive.content: The initial foot-insole design used long-tail FSRs, limiting the minimum design to approximately a men’s size 7. The scoliosis-brace work likewise began from an existing sensor concept that needed to be made smaller and more practical for use.

deepDive.label: CAD Development
deepDive.content: Switched the insole to short-tail FSRs, expanding the design down to approximately a men’s size 3. Built equation-driven SolidWorks geometry so shoe size and wire-routing features changed consistently together, and modeled separate bodies for conductive-TPU electrical connections.

deepDive.label: TPU Printing & Electronics Integration
deepDive.content: Developed multi-material printing workflows in which printing was paused so FSRs and embedded wires could be placed before being encapsulated by subsequent TPU layers. Also investigated printed-electronics approaches, including literature on colloidal silver for conductive traces.

deepDive.label: Instron Testing / Experimental Design
deepDive.content: Designed and ran force-sensor validation using an Instron. The experimental campaign included 125 trials across the FSRs, with data collected through the test setup and subsequently parsed in Excel.

deepDive.label: Testing Results
deepDive.content: Testing showed that the conductive-TPU connection was not sufficiently robust for consistent FSR readings, introducing variability that reduced confidence in center-of-pressure calculations.

deepDive.label: Serviceable Model
deepDive.content: Developed a serviceable insole version with a removable snap-on/snap-off cover so electrical connections could be accessed and adjusted instead of being permanently encapsulated.

deepDive.label: Scoliosis Brace Sensor
deepDive.content: Applied similar TPU-printing and Instron-validation methods to the scoliosis-brace sensor. Explored attachment methods including Velcro, skin-sensitive semi-reusable tape, and reusable/washable tape concepts. The final design was reviewed with Baylor Scott & White, validated on the Instron, and passed to the clinical team for testing.

deepDive.label: Future Considerations
deepDive.content: Future iterations would prioritize more robust electrical connections, potentially returning to soldered connections or connector-based approaches rather than relying on conductive TPU alone.

yellow.title: Yellow Jacket Competition Robot
yellow.summary: Competition robot that collected tennis balls, placed them on a Velcro wall, and climbed 15° and 30° inclines.
yellow.desc: A semester-long Turf Wars machine-design competition robot built to place tennis balls onto a wall with three scoring heights. Our team prioritized scoring quantity, ultimately developing an “egg-carton flipper” capable of placing four balls at once.
yellow.contrib: Developed 100% of the final robot CAD, helped prototype the mechanism in cardboard, and contributed substantially to manufacturing and assembly. The project introduced me to machining through operations including milling wheel molds, turning shafts, and fabricating angle-bracket components.

deepDive.label: Prototyping
deepDive.content: Explored several concepts, including elevator/waterwheel/conveyor-style mechanisms that transported balls individually and a spiral concept with similar functionality. The final direction was an “egg-carton flipper” that prioritized quantity and could place four balls simultaneously. We demonstrated the concept first with a cardboard prototype.

deepDive.label: CAD Development
deepDive.content: After validating the cardboard concept, I completed 100% of the CAD for the final design in SolidWorks, translating the prototype into a fully manufacturable robot assembly.

deepDive.label: Manufacturing Process
deepDive.content: Manufacturing included milling molds for cast-silicone wheels, turning rotational shafts, cutting angle-bracket components on the bandsaw, and assembling the mechanical system. This project was my introduction to machining and became the starting point for my later interest in manufacturing.

deepDive.label: Testing
deepDive.content: Tested the mechanism against the Turf Wars requirements, including tennis-ball placement at multiple scoring heights and operation over the course obstacles.

deepDive.label: Design Problems & Resolutions
deepDive.content: The main design tradeoff was scoring quantity versus individual placement precision. Rather than optimizing a one-ball-at-a-time mechanism, the final flipper architecture intentionally prioritized depositing multiple balls in a single action.

nerf.title: Red Light–Green Light Nerf Turret
nerf.summary: Squid Game-inspired Red Light–Green Light Nerf turret using five PIR sensors, Arduino logic, servos, and a rotating mechanical platform.
nerf.desc: A Red Light–Green Light-inspired mechatronics system that used five PIR sensors to detect motion during the green-light state and command a rotating Nerf turret to aim and fire. The project combined Arduino control logic, sensor segmentation, servo actuation, laser-cut structures, acrylic, and iterative mechanical troubleshooting.
nerf.contrib: Worked across both the electrical and mechanical systems: developed and expanded the PIR sensing logic, prototyped sensor view windows and aiming geometry, contributed to the laser-cut enclosure and rotating turret architecture, and helped troubleshoot actuator torque and late-stage mechanical failures during the SEAS Design Fair.
nerf.result: Functional course-final turret demonstrated at the SEAS Design Fair after rapid on-site mechanical repairs and actuator redesigns.

deepDive.label: Control Logic & PIR Prototyping
deepDive.content: The sensing system began with Arduino code for a single PIR sensor and was expanded to five sensors. The core behavior followed a state-based structure: during green light, PIR motion could trigger turret rotation, a delay, and then the firing servo; during red light, the system remained inactive.

deepDive.label: Mechanical Prototyping
deepDive.content: Because each PIR needed its own field of view, we first mocked up the sensor separation using Styrofoam. A paperclip was used as a simple visual indicator to verify that each sensor window was pointing in the intended direction before committing to the final structure.

deepDive.label: CAD & Mechanical Design
deepDive.content: Laser-cut wood panels created separate PIR viewing windows and enclosed the internal circuitry. The stop lights used hinged wooden structures with acrylic disks over the LED arrays to diffuse and reflect the light. The Nerf gun sat on an acrylic disk supported by a ball-bearing track to enable turret rotation.

deepDive.label: Actuation & Power Transmission
deepDive.content: The rotating turret and trigger were both servo-actuated. When the turret servo proved underpowered, we reduced rotating mass by adding weight-relief cuts to the acrylic support disk. For the trigger, weight reduction was not practical, so we added a gear train to increase available torque.

deepDive.label: Design Problems & Resolutions
deepDive.content: On the day of the SEAS Design Fair, the trigger motor exceeded its programmed limit, over-torqued, and tore off the custom attachment that interfaced with the Nerf gun. We recovered the system by drilling through both the gun and the attachment and securing them together with a zip tie. The project reinforced the need for mechanical stops, torque margin, and more deliberate transmission design; in a redesign, the turret itself would also use a gear train rather than relying primarily on weight reduction.

bridge.title: Optimized I-Beam Bridge
bridge.summary: Wood bridge optimized for compression force-to-weight performance and tested in an Instron.
bridge.desc: A wood-and-acrylic bridge designed for a structural competition and compression-tested on an Instron. The bridge carried 16 kN—the highest absolute load in the competition—but placed second because ranking was based on force-to-weight ratio.
bridge.contrib: Designed and fabricated the bridge around an I-beam-inspired cross section, considered wood grain direction during manufacturing to avoid weak orientations, and incorporated acrylic into the upper structure for aesthetics. The acrylic added weight without meaningful structural benefit, which reduced the final force-to-weight score.

deepDive.label: Structural Design
deepDive.content: Used an I-beam-inspired cross section to increase bending and compressive performance while controlling mass.

deepDive.label: Material & Manufacturing Decisions
deepDive.content: Built primarily from wood with wood-glue assembly and intentionally oriented the wood grain to avoid creating weak directions. Acrylic was incorporated into the upper section for visual appeal.

deepDive.label: Instron Testing
deepDive.content: Compression-tested the completed bridge on an Instron. It sustained 16 kN, the highest absolute force in the competition.

deepDive.label: Outcome & Lessons
deepDive.content: The competition was scored by force-to-weight ratio, so the bridge placed second despite carrying the highest load. The acrylic aesthetic feature added mass without structural benefit, making it a clear lesson in aligning every design decision with the actual optimization metric.

egg.title: Variable-Damping Egg Drop System
egg.summary: Spring-damper protection system using shaped tracks to vary damping behavior through compression.
egg.desc: A dynamics competition project using springs, dampers, and laser-cut wood to protect an egg during impact. The damper traveled along mathematically designed tracks so its compression behavior varied through the impact stroke.
egg.contrib: Helped develop the mathematically driven variable-damping concept, fabricate the laser-cut structure, and test the system. The project also became a useful lesson in the difference between idealized models and real hardware behavior.

deepDive.label: System Concept
deepDive.content: Designed an impact-mitigation system around springs and dampers so an egg could survive drops from increasing heights.

deepDive.label: Variable Damping Geometry
deepDive.content: Connected the end of the damper to a shaped track derived from the system mathematics. As the structure compressed, the track changed how the damper was actuated with the goal of keeping egg acceleration as low as possible.

deepDive.label: Manufacturing
deepDive.content: Fabricated the structure using laser-cut wood and assembled the spring-damper mechanism and shaped tracks.

deepDive.label: Testing & Reality vs. Model
deepDive.content: The ideal analysis assumed behavior such as a frictionless track, while the physical system introduced imperfections that changed the response. During competition, a corner of the structure broke on impact and absorbed a large amount of energy—effectively acting as sacrificial structure—and the egg survived.

deepDive.label: Outcome
deepDive.content: Placed second in the competition. The result highlighted both the value and limitations of idealized dynamics models when implemented in imperfect physical hardware.

abaqus.title: Parametric Abaqus Unit-Cell Compression Model
abaqus.summary: Python-driven Abaqus model varying side count, radius, and height to study compression response.
abaqus.desc: A parametric Abaqus compression model for studying how unit-cell geometry affects mechanical response. A Python-based geometry system allowed the number of sides, radius, and height to be varied systematically.
abaqus.contrib: Developed the Python-driven parametric geometry and compression model, representing cell edges as spring-like structural members and enabling controlled comparison across geometric configurations.

deepDive.label: Model Architecture
deepDive.content: Developed a compression model in Abaqus that represents the unit-cell edges as individual spring-like structural members.

deepDive.label: Python Parametric Geometry
deepDive.content: Built a Python-based geometry workflow so the model could be varied programmatically rather than rebuilt manually.

deepDive.label: Design Variables
deepDive.content: Made the number of sides, radius, and height controllable parameters so their influence on compression behavior could be compared systematically.

deepDive.label: Analysis
deepDive.content: Used the parameterized model to compare the efficacy and mechanical response of unit-cell configurations as the selected geometric variables changed.

controls.title: Friction & Backlash Compensation Test Platform
controls.summary: Experimental controls platform that varied friction and backlash in a brushless-motor transmission, then used collected data to develop a PID controller with compensation.
controls.desc: For the ES-159 final project, we designed a data-collection platform that let us deliberately vary friction and backlash in the power transmission between a brushless motor and an incremental encoder. We used the measured system response to characterize how these non-idealities affected motion and then developed a PID controller that incorporated friction and backlash compensation.
controls.contrib: Designed and built the adjustable experimental system, helped define how friction and backlash would be introduced through the transmission, collected response data from the motor/encoder setup, analyzed the resulting behavior, and contributed to development of the compensated PID controller.
controls.result: Course final project demonstrating data-driven friction and backlash compensation in closed-loop control.

deepDive.label: System Architecture
deepDive.content: Developed a test platform centered on a brushless motor and incremental encoder, with a power-transmission arrangement that could be changed to introduce controlled amounts of friction and backlash.

deepDive.label: Experimental Design
deepDive.content: Structured the system so friction and backlash could be varied independently enough to observe their effect on the measured response rather than treating them only as theoretical disturbances.

deepDive.label: Data Collection
deepDive.content: Collected motor/encoder response data across the different mechanical conditions to build an empirical picture of how the system changed as friction and backlash increased.

deepDive.label: Controller Development
deepDive.content: Used the measured data to develop a PID controller and augment it with compensation terms intended to reduce the effects of friction and backlash in the physical system.

deepDive.label: Validation & Lessons
deepDive.content: Compared system response under different mechanical conditions and used the results to evaluate how well the compensation strategy addressed real transmission non-idealities.

plasma.title: 3-Axis CNC Plasma Cutter
plasma.summary: In-progress 3-axis CNC plasma cutter using a removable hand torch, belt-driven NEMA axes, V-slot/8020 motion hardware, Arduino/GRBL controls, and planned automatic torch-height probing.
plasma.desc: An in-progress custom 3-axis CNC plasma cutter designed around a standard removable hand-held plasma torch. The machine is intended to automate XY cutting and Z-axis focus while preserving the torch's ability to be removed and used independently. The control architecture uses Arduino/GRBL, while the user interface is planned to be hosted through a GitHub repository.
plasma.contrib: Designed the machine architecture, motion system, removable torch integration, 3D-printed components, Z-axis focus concept, and controls approach. I am also developing the Arduino/GRBL workflow and the planned user interface.
plasma.result: Active personal build; target completion December 2026.

deepDive.label: System Concept
deepDive.content: The machine uses a standard hand-held plasma torch mounted to the CNC end effector so the torch can be removed and used independently. The goal is to gain CNC capability without permanently modifying or dedicating the existing plasma cutter.

deepDive.label: Mechanical Architecture
deepDive.content: All three axes use belt-driven motion with V-slot wheels riding on aluminum extrusion and NEMA stepper motors providing actuation. Custom structural and interface parts are designed for 3D-printed PLA, while the aluminum extrusion is cut to length for the frame.

deepDive.label: Z-Axis & Torch Height
deepDive.content: The end effector includes a motor-driven lead-screw linear actuator for focus/height adjustment. The planned automatic-focus workflow uses material thickness as an input and adds a probing sensor on the Z axis to establish the work surface.

deepDive.label: Controls & GRBL
deepDive.content: Machine motion is programmed around Arduino and the GRBL controller. The interface is planned to accept job/material information and coordinate axis motion through the standard GRBL workflow.

deepDive.label: Plasma-Cutter Integration
deepDive.content: Because the plasma cutter cannot be electrically modified, the software will recommend torch settings based on the selected material and thickness, but the user will set those parameters manually. The machine can indicate when it is ready to cut, while plasma ignition remains a separate manual action.

deepDive.label: User Interface
deepDive.content: The planned user interface will be hosted from a GitHub repository and will provide a cleaner front end for machine setup, material inputs, and the CNC workflow.

deepDive.label: Current Status
deepDive.content: Mechanical design and manufacturing are underway. The current target is to complete the machine by December 2026, followed by calibration, probing integration, and cutting validation.

stocksmart.title: StockSmart — Wyss Institute Storage Solution
stocksmart.summary: A new storage solution designed for the Wyss Institute at Harvard to address problems caused by disproportionate billing.
stocksmart.desc: A semester-long client-driven design project for the Wyss Institute focused on an inefficient stock-room system that could cause labs to be billed disproportionately relative to the supplies they actually used.
stocksmart.contrib: Helped conduct client and problem research, evaluate multiple possible problem statements, and develop StockSmart: an NFC-based inventory workflow using pre-programmed phones, a front-end application, and a back-end website designed to remain adaptable as stock-room supplies change.
stocksmart.result: Semester-long class design project for the Wyss Institute at Harvard

deepDive.label: Client Research & Problem Definition
deepDive.content: Conducted research on the Wyss Institute and its stock-room workflow to identify problems where an engineering design intervention could be useful. The team considered multiple possible problem statements before focusing on disproportionate billing and inventory tracking.

deepDive.label: System Concept
deepDive.content: Developed StockSmart as a replacement inventory workflow centered on NFC chip scanning and pre-programmed phones.

deepDive.label: Front-End / Back-End System
deepDive.content: The proposed solution included a developed front-end application and supporting back-end website to connect user interactions with stock-room records.

deepDive.label: Adaptability
deepDive.content: Designed the system around future maintainability so inventory items and supplies could be updated as the stock room changes rather than requiring a fixed one-time implementation.

square-pendulum.title: Square Pendulum Normal Modes
square-pendulum.summary: Combined analytical, MATLAB, and physical modeling study of the normal modes of a square pendulum system.
square-pendulum.desc: A Wave Phenomena project investigating the normal modes of a square pendulum rather than a conventional single pendulum. We developed a mathematical model in MATLAB, used it to predict the system's characteristic motions, and then compared those predictions with the behavior of the physical setup.
square-pendulum.contrib: Contributed to the mathematical formulation, MATLAB implementation, physical model, experimental observation, and comparison between predicted and measured normal-mode behavior.
square-pendulum.result: Course project and presentation comparing predicted and observed normal modes.

deepDive.label: Research Question
deepDive.content: Investigated how the coupled geometry of a square pendulum changes the system's normal modes relative to a standard single-pendulum model.

deepDive.label: Mathematical Model
deepDive.content: Developed the mathematical relationships needed to predict the characteristic motions of the square-pendulum system.

deepDive.label: MATLAB Development
deepDive.content: Implemented the model in MATLAB to generate predictions for the normal modes and provide a reference for the physical experiment.

deepDive.label: Physical Experiment
deepDive.content: Built and observed the real square-pendulum system, exciting the structure and identifying motion patterns that could be compared with the model predictions.

deepDive.label: Model vs. Experiment
deepDive.content: Compared the predicted MATLAB behavior with the experimentally observed modes. Additional technical detail is preserved in the linked class presentation/poster.

heat-transfer.title: Infrared Imaging as an Indicator of Plant Drought Stress
heat-transfer.summary: Two-week experiment using six fern plants, controlled watering levels, and daily IR imaging to investigate whether thermal imagery can reveal drought stress before plant death.
heat-transfer.desc: A semester-long heat-transfer investigation into whether infrared imaging could serve as an indicator of plant drought stress. After an initial field-based concept produced too little controlled variation, the project was redesigned as a controlled fern experiment.
heat-transfer.contrib: Co-developed the experimental redesign, maintained controlled environmental conditions, varied water input as the independent variable, collected IR imagery as the dependent measurement, and analyzed the resulting thermal behavior.

deepDive.label: Initial Research Question
deepDive.content: The initial concept was to investigate trees in a natural environment for thermal signatures associated with water stress.

deepDive.label: Experimental Redesign
deepDive.content: Field measurements lacked sufficient control over environmental variables to produce meaningful conclusions, so the study was redesigned around six fern plants in a controlled setting.

deepDive.label: Controlled Variables
deepDive.content: Water amount was varied as the independent variable and IR-imaging results were treated as the dependent variable. Other factors, including temperature and light exposure, were held as consistent as possible across plants.

deepDive.label: Data Collection
deepDive.content: Collected daily infrared images over the experimental period while maintaining the assigned watering conditions for each fern.

deepDive.label: Analysis Goal
deepDive.content: Evaluated whether thermal-image changes could provide an early indication of drought stress before severe visible decline or plant death.

machining-projects.title: Machining Projects — Brass Hammer
machining-projects.summary: Decorative brass hammer made on a manual lathe as a turning-practice project, using stepped geometry and hand finishing to create an ornate handle profile.
machining-projects.desc: A manual-lathe practice project focused on building turning skill through a small finished object. I made an ornate brass hammer with a handle inspired by candlesticks and decorative furniture legs, including a beaded profile produced through closely spaced stepped cuts and hand finishing.
machining-projects.contrib: Designed the visual profile, turned the brass components manually, created the decorative handle geometry through many small diameter steps, and progressively sanded the transitions until the stepped geometry became a smooth ornamental contour.

deepDive.label: Design Inspiration
deepDive.content: The handle profile was inspired by the ornamental forms found in candlesticks and turned table or chair legs, rather than a purely utilitarian hammer handle.

deepDive.label: Manual Turning
deepDive.content: The project was made on a manual lathe as deliberate practice in controlling diameters, shoulders, and surface finish in brass.

deepDive.label: Decorative Profile
deepDive.content: I created the beaded/ornamental section as a series of very small stepped diameter changes, gradually reducing the size of the steps to approximate the intended curved profile.

deepDive.label: Finishing
deepDive.content: The stepped surfaces were then sanded until the transitions blended into a continuous smooth contour, turning the discrete lathe cuts into the final decorative form.

mccannic-vehicle-mover.title: Shop Vehicle-Moving Grill Guard
mccannic-vehicle-mover.summary: MIG-welded angle-iron front attachment with tire sections used to push disabled vehicles short distances around an automotive repair shop.
mccannic-vehicle-mover.desc: A shop-fabrication project created to make it faster and easier to reposition disabled vehicles around an automotive repair facility without setting up a tow for every short movement. The device used a rigid angle-iron frame attached to the front of a shop truck, with tire sections providing a more compliant contact surface against the vehicle being moved.
mccannic-vehicle-mover.contrib: Cut, fit, and MIG-welded the angle-iron structure and helped assemble the tire-contact portions into the completed front-mounted vehicle-moving device.
mccannic-vehicle-mover.result: Completed shop tool used to move broken-down vehicles around the repair facility.

deepDive.label: Problem & Use Case
deepDive.content: The auto-repair shop needed a quick way to move disabled vehicles short distances around the property without repeatedly setting up conventional towing equipment.

deepDive.label: Concept
deepDive.content: The solution was a front-mounted steel guard on a shop truck that could contact and push another vehicle, with cut tire sections acting as compliant interfaces to reduce direct metal-to-vehicle contact.

deepDive.label: Fabrication
deepDive.content: The structure was built from angle iron that was cut, fitted, and MIG-welded into the front-mounted frame.

deepDive.label: Implementation
deepDive.content: Tire sections were attached to the completed guard, and the truck was then used as a practical shop vehicle mover for broken-down cars.
